content: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a Gram-negative, non-motile, encapsulated, rod-shaped bacterium that ferments lactose and is facultatively anaerobic. It is commonly found as part of the normal flora in the mouth, skin, and intestines. This bacterium is the most clinically significant member of the Klebsiella genus within the Enterobacteriaceae family. It is closely related to Klebsiella oxytoca but can be distinguished by its indole-negative status and its ability to grow on melezitose and 3-hydroxybutyrate. Klebsiella pneumoniae naturally occurs in soil, and approximately 30% of its strains are capable of fixing nitrogen under anaerobic conditions. As a free-living diazotroph, its nitrogen fixation system has been extensively studied. However, new antibiotic-resistant strains of Klebsiella pneumoniae are emerging, and it is increasingly identified as a cause of nosocomial infections. The Gram staining technique, developed in 1884 by Danish scientist Hans Christian Gram, was originally used to differentiate Klebsiella pneumoniae from Streptococcus pneumoniae. The genus Klebsiella was named after the German bacteriologist Edwin Klebs. Community-acquired pneumonia caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae is sometimes referred to as Friedländer's pneumonia, named after Carl Friedländer. Klebsiella pneumoniae can cause bacterial pneumonia, often due to aspiration in individuals with alcoholism. However, it is more commonly associated with hospital-acquired infections, such as urinary tract infections (UTIs) and wound infections, particularly in immunocompromised patients. Among older adults, Klebsiella ranks second only to Escherichia coli as a cause of UTIs. It is also an opportunistic pathogen in individuals with chronic pulmonary disease, enteric pathogenicity, nasal mucosa atrophy, and rhinoscleroma. The primary source of patient infections is fecal contamination, followed by contact with contaminated medical instruments. Klebsiella species typically express two types of antigens on their cell surface. The first is the O antigen, a lipopolysaccharide with 77 known varieties. The second is the K antigen, a capsular polysaccharide with nine varieties. Both antigens contribute to the bacterium's pathogenicity and are used for subtyping. Research at King’s College London has implicated molecular mimicry between HLA-B27 and two molecules in Klebsiella microbes as a potential cause of ankylosing spondylitis. In general, Klebsiella infections tend to occur in individuals with weakened immune systems, often due to poor diet or other underlying conditions. Many infections are acquired during hospital stays for unrelated reasons. Outside of hospital settings, pneumonia is the most common infection caused by Klebsiella bacteria, particularly in individuals with underlying conditions such as alcoholism, diabetes, or chronic lung disease. Klebsiella pneumoniae possesses a chromosomal class A beta-lactamase enzyme, which provides inherent resistance to ampicillin. Many strains have acquired extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs), conferring additional resistance to antibiotics such as carbenicillin, ampicillin, quinolones, and increasingly ceftazidime. However, the bacteria remain largely susceptible to aminoglycosides and cephalosporins. Variable inhibition of beta-lactamase activity with clavulanic acid has been reported. The emergence of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens in intensive care units (ICUs) has led to the renewed use of colistin, an antibiotic that had been rarely used for decades. However, colistin-resistant strains of Klebsiella pneumoniae have also been identified. For infections caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae, particularly those involving ESBL-producing strains in pneumonia, sepsis, complicated UTIs, or intra-abdominal infections, the following antimicrobial regimens are preferred: 1. Imipenem 500 mg IV every 6 hours 2. Meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours 3. Ertapenem 1 g IV every 24 hours 4. Doripenem 500 mg IV every 8 hours It is important to note that in ESBL-producing strains, inconsistent activity is observed with aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and piperacillin-tazobactam. Cephalosporins should be avoided in these cases.
